questions.q: In a healthy 70 kg adult male, what is the approximate total body water (TBW) expressed as a percentage of body weight and in liters?
questions.explain: Total body water averages 60% of body weight in an adult male (0.60 x 70 kg = 42 L), divided into two-thirds intracellular fluid (28 L) and one-third extracellular fluid (14 L).

open.q: State the normal total body water volume in liters and as a percentage of body weight for a standard 70 kg adult male.

questions.q: Why is total body water as a percentage of body weight lower in adult females (about 50%) than in adult males (about 60%)?
options: Females have a larger plasma volume per kilogram
A higher average proportion of adipose tissue lowers total body water as a fraction of body weight
Females have more skeletal muscle relative to body weight
Females secrete more aldosterone at baseline
questions.explain: Adipose tissue is roughly 10% water compared to about 73% in lean skeletal muscle; because women typically have higher body fat percentages, their TBW averages 50% of body weight.

open.q: Why does total body water account for a smaller percentage of body weight in adult females (~50%) than in adult males (~60%)?
accept: Adipose tissue contains very little water

questions.q: Which population group has the highest total body water percentage relative to total body weight?
questions.explain: Newborn infants have a TBW of approximately 75% to 80% of body weight due to low body fat and relatively expanded extracellular fluid, whereas TBW declines to ~45-50% in old age.

open.q: Which age group has the highest total body water as a percentage of body weight (approximately 75% to 80%)?

questions.q: According to the 60-40-20 rule in a 70 kg adult male, how is the 14 L of extracellular fluid (ECF) partitioned between interstitial fluid and plasma?
options: 7 L interstitial fluid and 7 L plasma
3.5 L interstitial fluid and 10.5 L plasma
12 L interstitial fluid and 2 L plasma
10.5 L interstitial fluid and 3.5 L plasma
questions.explain: Extracellular fluid (20% of body weight = 14 L) consists of roughly three-fourths interstitial fluid (15% of body weight = 10.5 L) and one-fourth intravascular plasma (5% of body weight = 3.5 L).

open.q: In a 70 kg adult male with 14 L of extracellular fluid, how many liters are in the interstitial compartment versus the plasma compartment?
accept: 10.5 L interstitial fluid and 3.5 L plasma

questions.q: Which fluid belongs to the transcellular fluid compartment?
questions.explain: Transcellular fluids (about 1 to 2 L) are specialized extracellular fluids separated from plasma by an epithelial cell layer, including CSF, synovial, pleural, pericardial, peritoneal, and intraocular fluids.

open.q: Give two examples of fluids that belong to the transcellular fluid compartment.

questions.q: What are the predominant cation and predominant anion in the extracellular fluid (ECF)?
questions.explain: ECF is rich in Na+ (~142 mEq/L) as its principal cation and Cl- (~103 mEq/L) followed by HCO3- (~24 mEq/L) as its main anions.

open.q: Name the predominant cation and the predominant anion in human extracellular fluid.

questions.q: What are the predominant cation and major intracellular anions within the intracellular fluid (ICF)?
options: K+ and organic phosphates and proteins
questions.explain: ICF contains high concentrations of K+ (~140-150 mEq/L) and Mg2+, balanced mainly by negatively charged organic phosphates (ATP, creatine phosphate) and intracellular proteins.

open.q: Name the major cation and the two principal classes of anions found inside the intracellular fluid.
accept: Potassium with organic phosphates and proteins

questions.q: How does the composition of interstitial fluid differ most significantly from that of blood plasma?
options: Interstitial fluid has twice the sodium concentration of plasma
Interstitial fluid contains ten times more potassium than plasma
Interstitial fluid lacks glucose and urea
Interstitial fluid contains much less protein because capillary walls restrict plasma proteins
questions.explain: Capillary endothelium restricts large anionic plasma proteins (especially albumin), so plasma has ~7 g/dL protein while interstitial fluid has ~2 g/dL; consequently, via the Gibbs-Donnan effect, interstitial fluid has slightly higher Cl- and slightly lower Na+ than plasma.

open.q: What is the main compositional difference between blood plasma and interstitial fluid?
accept: Plasma has a much higher protein concentration
Interstitial fluid contains very little protein compared to plasma

questions.q: Because anionic plasma proteins cannot freely cross the capillary wall, diffusible anions such as Cl- are slightly more concentrated in interstitial fluid than in plasma. Which physical principle accounts for this asymmetric ion distribution?
questions.explain: The Gibbs-Donnan effect states that when a non-diffusible polyanion (plasma protein) is confined to one side of a semipermeable membrane, diffusible cations (Na+) are slightly higher on the protein side and diffusible anions (Cl-) are slightly higher on the protein-free side while maintaining electroneutrality.

open.q: Name the electrochemical equilibrium phenomenon caused by non-diffusible plasma proteins that creates slight differences in Na+ and Cl- concentrations between plasma and interstitial fluid.

questions.q: Which formula is used in the indicator-dilution principle to calculate the volume of a body fluid compartment?
options: Volume = Final tracer concentration / Amount of tracer injected
Volume = (Amount of tracer injected - Amount excreted) / Equilibrium plasma concentration
Volume = Amount excreted x Equilibrium plasma concentration
Volume = (Initial concentration + Final concentration) / Amount injected
questions.explain: By conservation of mass, V = (Q_administered - Q_excreted or metabolized) / C_equilibrium, provided the tracer distributes exclusively and uniformly within the target compartment.

open.q: Write the indicator-dilution formula used to measure the volume of a body fluid compartment when some indicator is excreted during equilibration.
accept: Volume = (Amount injected - Amount excreted) / Final concentration

questions.q: Which set of indicator substances is suitable for measuring total body water (TBW)?
options: Evans blue dye and I-125 labeled albumin
Tritiated water (3H2O), deuterium oxide (D2O), and antipyrine
questions.explain: Tritiated water, heavy water (D2O), and lipid-soluble antipyrine cross both capillary walls and cell membranes freely to equilibrate throughout all water compartments.

open.q: Name two tracer substances used to measure total body water by the indicator-dilution method.

questions.q: Which marker is classically used to measure extracellular fluid (ECF) volume because it crosses capillary endothelia but cannot enter cells?
questions.explain: Inulin (as well as mannitol, sucrose, and radiosulfate) diffuses freely across capillary pores into the interstitial space but is excluded by cell membranes, accurately measuring ECF volume.

open.q: Name a standard indicator substance used to measure extracellular fluid volume.

questions.q: Which indicator binds tightly to plasma albumin and therefore remains confined within the intravascular plasma compartment?
questions.explain: Evans blue dye binds avidly to serum albumin (or I-125 radioiodinated human serum albumin is used directly), restricting distribution to plasma.

open.q: Name the dye that binds to plasma albumin to measure plasma volume via indicator dilution.

questions.q: Why cannot intracellular fluid (ICF) volume and interstitial fluid (ISF) volume be measured directly with a single injected indicator?
options: Tracers are immediately destroyed by plasma enzymes
ICF and interstitial fluid cannot be measured directly with one tracer; derive them from total body water and ECF
ICF and interstitial fluid have identical protein concentrations
Interstitial fluid does not exchange with plasma
questions.explain: Any tracer injected into blood must pass through plasma and interstitial fluid before entering cells; hence ICF = TBW - ECF, and ISF = ECF - Plasma volume.

open.q: How are intracellular fluid (ICF) volume and interstitial fluid (ISF) volume determined experimentally from measured compartment volumes?
accept: ICF = TBW - ECF and ISF = ECF - Plasma volume
By subtraction: ICF equals TBW minus ECF, and ISF equals ECF minus plasma

questions.q: A 70 kg patient has a measured plasma volume of 3.0 L and a venous hematocrit of 0.40 (40%). What is the patient's estimated total blood volume?
questions.explain: Total Blood Volume = Plasma Volume / (1 - Hematocrit) = 3.0 L / (1 - 0.40) = 3.0 / 0.60 = 5.0 L.

open.q: Calculate total blood volume if plasma volume is 3.0 L and hematocrit is 40% (0.40).

questions.q: In an indicator-dilution test, 150 mg of inulin is injected intravenously. After equilibration, 30 mg has been excreted in the urine and the plasma inulin concentration is 0.01 mg/mL. What is the extracellular fluid volume?
questions.explain: Remaining inulin = 150 mg - 30 mg = 120 mg. Volume = 120 mg / 0.01 mg/mL = 12,000 mL = 12.0 L.

open.q: If 150 mg of inulin is injected, 30 mg is excreted in urine, and the equilibrium plasma concentration is 0.01 mg/mL, what is the extracellular fluid volume in liters?

questions.q: What is the normal plasma osmolarity in humans, and which solute accounts for nearly half of it?
options: About 285–295 mOsm/L; sodium and accompanying anions account for most of it
questions.explain: Normal plasma osmolarity is ~285-295 mOsm/L (estimated by 2[Na+] + Glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 in mg/dL); Na+ (~142 mEq/L) and its associated anions (Cl- and HCO3-) contribute roughly 280 mOsm/L.

open.q: State the normal plasma osmolarity range in humans and name the primary extracellular cation responsible for it.

questions.q: Intravenous infusion of 2 liters of isotonic 0.9% NaCl (normal saline) produces which change in intracellular fluid (ICF) and extracellular fluid (ECF) volumes?
options: ECF increases by 1 L and ICF increases by 1 L
ECF increases by 2 L and ICF remains unchanged
ECF decreases by 2 L and ICF increases by 2 L
Both ECF and ICF osmolarity rise sharply while volumes stay constant
questions.explain: Isotonic NaCl has the same effective osmolarity as body fluids and remains confined to the extracellular compartment; because there is no osmotic gradient across cell membranes, zero water enters or leaves ICF.

open.q: When 2 L of isotonic 0.9% NaCl is infused intravenously, how do extracellular fluid volume, intracellular fluid volume, and plasma osmolarity change?
accept: ECF increases by 2 L, ICF is unchanged, and osmolarity is unchanged
All 2 L stays in ECF with no change in ICF or osmolarity

questions.q: A patient loses 1.5 liters of pure water through profuse sweating in extreme heat without replacing fluids (hyperosmotic volume contraction). How do the fluid compartments change?
options: Only ECF volume falls while ICF volume expands
ECF osmolarity falls while ICF osmolarity rises
Water shifts from ICF to ECF; both compartments shrink and osmolarity rises
ICF volume remains constant while ECF falls
questions.explain: Pure water loss concentrates the ECF, creating an osmotic gradient that pulls water out of cells into the ECF until both compartments equilibrate at a higher osmolarity and reduced volume.

open.q: In pure water dehydration (hyperosmotic volume contraction), what happens to ECF volume, ICF volume, and body fluid osmolarity?
accept: Both ECF and ICF volumes decrease while osmolarity increases in both
ECF and ICF shrink and osmolarity rises

questions.q: In untreated adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), renal sodium wasting causes hyposmotic volume contraction. What happens to intracellular fluid (ICF) volume and osmolarity?
options: ICF volume decreases and ICF osmolarity increases
Both ICF volume and ICF osmolarity remain unchanged
ICF volume decreases and ICF osmolarity decreases
ICF volume increases (cells swell) and ICF osmolarity decreases
questions.explain: Loss of NaCl in excess of water lowers ECF osmolarity, driving water osmotically from the hypotonic ECF into cells; consequently, ECF shrinks markedly while ICF expands and overall body fluid osmolarity falls.

open.q: In hyposmotic volume contraction caused by net NaCl loss, in which direction does water shift between ECF and ICF, and what happens to ICF volume?
accept: Water shifts from ECF into ICF, increasing ICF volume
Water enters cells and ICF volume expands

questions.q: Intravenous infusion of 5% dextrose in water (D5W) initially acts as an isotonic solution in the IV bag, but once the glucose is metabolized by cells, what is its net physiological effect on fluid compartments?
options: After glucose metabolism, D5W acts as free water and distributes across ECF and ICF
It remains exclusively in the intravascular plasma space
It draws water out of cells and raises plasma osmolarity
It expands only interstitial fluid while shrinking plasma
questions.explain: Once cellular uptake and metabolism clear the dextrose, only free water remains, which distributes across total body water in proportion to compartment sizes (~2/3 ICF, 1/3 ECF) and reduces osmolarity.

open.q: After the infused glucose in 5% dextrose in water (D5W) is metabolized by cells, how does the remaining water distribute between ECF and ICF?
accept: Distributes across both ECF and ICF like pure water (1/3 ECF, 2/3 ICF)
Expands both ECF and ICF proportionally and lowers osmolarity

questions.q: Which Starling force favors the reabsorption of fluid from the interstitial space back into the blood capillary?
questions.explain: Plasma colloid osmotic pressure (~25-28 mmHg), generated chiefly by serum albumin, draws water osmotically into the capillary lumen; Pc, pi_i, and negative Pi all favor filtration out of the capillary.

open.q: Name the primary Starling force responsible for pulling interstitial fluid back into capillaries at their venular end.

questions.q: Which protein accounts for approximately 75% to 80% of plasma colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure?
questions.explain: Albumin has the highest molar concentration among plasma proteins and carries a strong net negative charge that attracts Na+ cations (Gibbs-Donnan contribution), generating about 75-80% of plasma oncotic pressure.

open.q: Name the plasma protein responsible for roughly 75% to 80% of plasma colloid osmotic pressure.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child with severe protein-energy malnutrition (kwashiorkor) develops generalized pitting edema and ascites. Which alteration in Starling forces is the primary cause of this edema?
options: Obstruction of major lymphatic trunks by parasites
Decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure due to hypoalbuminemia
questions.explain: Severe dietary protein deficiency impairs hepatic albumin synthesis, lowering plasma oncotic pressure so net outward filtration exceeds lymphatic drainage capacity and fluid accumulates in the interstitial and peritoneal spaces.

open.q: In kwashiorkor or nephrotic syndrome, which Starling force abnormality directly causes generalized pitting edema?
accept: Reduced plasma colloid osmotic pressure from hypoalbuminemia

questions.q: A 38-year-old resident of an endemic tropical region develops chronic unilateral lower-limb non-pitting swelling (elephantiasis) due to Wuchereria bancrofti infection. Which mechanism produces this edema?
options: Lymphatic obstruction prevents clearance of filtered fluid and interstitial proteins
Severe hypoalbuminaemia from renal protein loss
Systemic venous hypertension from left ventricular failure
questions.explain: Filariasis obstructs lymphatic drainage, trapping filtered fluid and leaked interstitial proteins in the tissue spaces; rising interstitial protein further elevates interstitial oncotic pressure and draws more water out of capillaries.

open.q: How does lymphatic obstruction (such as in filariasis or after axillary lymph node dissection) lead to lymphedema?
accept: Impaired drainage of excess interstitial fluid and leaked proteins
Failure of lymphatics to return filtered fluid and proteins to the circulation
